item.title: Keeping Angular Tabs in Sync with BroadcastChannel and Signals
item.content:encoded:
A small example with a shared preference, persistent state, and no message loops.

Let’s say our application has a menu with a “Show only pinned items” setting. We open the application in two tabs, change the setting in one, and expect the other to follow.

Inside each tab, an Angular service can hold the setting in a signal. But each tab runs its own application and has its own service instance. Changing one signal does not update the other.

Let’s connect them with BroadcastChannel and keep the example small: one setting, one service, and one checkbox.

The code below targets an existing Angular application with client rendering. It assumes a browser with working BroadcastChannel and localStorage access. Applications with server rendering need a browser-only boundary around this service.

What should each part do?

We will use localStorage to keep the current preference, BroadcastChannel to tell other tabs that it changed, and a signal to expose the value to Angular templates.

The message will contain only the kind of change. When another tab receives it, that tab reads the current value from storage.

Why read it again? A message may be handled after another write has already happened. Reading storage avoids replacing the current preference with an older value carried by a delayed notification.

BroadcastChannel connects listeners using the same channel name. The sending channel object does not receive its own message, so we must update the originating tab ourselves. This example uses ordinary same-origin tabs in the same browser profile; embedded pages can have additional storage-partition restrictions.

Create the service

Put the service in src/app/menu-preferences.service.ts:

import { DestroyRef, Injectable, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';

const STORAGE_KEY = 'demo:menu:pinned-only';
const CHANNEL_NAME = 'demo:menu-preferences:v1';
type PreferenceChanged = {
  type: 'pinned-only-changed';
};

function isPreferenceChanged(value: unknown): value is PreferenceChanged {
  return (
    typeof value === 'object' &&
    value !== null &&
    'type' in value &&
    value.type === 'pinned-only-changed'
  );
}

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class MenuPreferencesService {
  private readonly channel = new BroadcastChannel(CHANNEL_NAME);
  private readonly destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef);
  private readonly pinnedOnlyState = signal(this.readPinnedOnly());
  readonly pinnedOnly = this.pinnedOnlyState.asReadonly();

  constructor() {
    this.channel.onmessage = ({ data }: MessageEvent<unknown>) => {
      if (isPreferenceChanged(data)) {
        this.refresh();
      }
    };
    this.destroyRef.onDestroy(() => this.channel.close());
  }

  setPinnedOnly(value: boolean): void {
    localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, String(value));
    this.refresh();
    this.channel.postMessage({
      type: 'pinned-only-changed',
    } satisfies PreferenceChanged);
  }

  private refresh(): void {
    this.pinnedOnlyState.set(this.readPinnedOnly());
  }

  private readPinnedOnly(): boolean {
    return localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY) === 'true';
  }
}

There are two paths through this service.

A local change calls setPinnedOnly(): it saves the preference, refreshes the local signal, and sends a notification. An incoming notification calls refresh(): it only reads storage and updates the signal.

That difference prevents a loop. Receiving a message never sends another message, and it never writes an old value back to storage. Keep postMessage() on the local-change path. An effect that broadcasts every signal update would also broadcast changes received from other tabs.

The writable signal is private. Components get a read-only view and use setPinnedOnly() to change the setting, so they cannot accidentally skip persistence or notification.

DestroyRef closes the channel when the service’s injector is destroyed. Since this service uses providedIn: 'root', its lifetime is tied to the application, not to one checkbox component.

Connect a component

Use this standalone component in src/app/app.component.ts:

import { ChangeDetectionStrategy, Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { MenuPreferencesService } from './menu-preferences.service';
@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  standalone: true,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <label>
      <input
        #checkbox
        type="checkbox"
        [checked]="preferences.pinnedOnly()"
        (change)="preferences.setPinnedOnly(checkbox.checked)"
      />
      Show only pinned items
    </label>
    <p>
      Current preference:
      {{ preferences.pinnedOnly() ? 'Pinned items only' : 'All items' }}
    </p>
  `,
})
export class AppComponent {
  protected readonly preferences = inject(MenuPreferencesService);
}

Bootstrap it as the root of a client-rendered Angular application. A minimal src/main.ts is:

import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { AppComponent } from './app/app.component';
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent).catch(console.error);

The template reads the signal directly. Angular tracks signal reads in templates, so changing the signal marks this OnPush component for an update.

The message handler runs outside the Angular zone: Zone.js does not patch the onmessage property of BroadcastChannel. That is fine. Since Angular 18, a signal update schedules change detection on its own, so the same code works with the default Zone.js setup and with zoneless change detection.

The component does not need to know whether the change came from its own checkbox or another tab.

Try it with two tabs

Open the running application at the same URL in two tabs. Check the box in the first tab: the second tab should update too. Uncheck it in the second tab and watch the first one follow.

Now open a third tab or reload one of the existing tabs. The preference is restored from localStorage. BroadcastChannel does not replay earlier messages; storage supplies the initial value. This initialization also works when none of the earlier tabs are still open.

A few boundaries

For this single stored boolean, the browser’s storage event is also a reasonable choice. BroadcastChannel is useful when you want explicit application messages, such as a preference change or a request to refresh data. You do not need both notification mechanisms for this example.

All writes to this preference should go through the service. A direct localStorage.setItem() elsewhere will not send our channel notification.

If two tabs write at nearly the same time, they read whichever value is currently stored when they refresh. This example does not merge edits or coordinate transactions. The channel provides live notifications without acknowledgements or a durable message queue. It also does not synchronize different devices. A shared document or a server-owned setting needs its own conflict and persistence rules.

Finally, the signal represents the current preference. If every individual event matters, process those events directly or use an event stream. A signal holding the latest message is not an event history, and toObservable can combine several signal updates into one emission.

With these boundaries, the same pattern works for small browser-local preferences such as compact mode or a selected display option. Keep the write path explicit, let incoming messages refresh state, and let Angular render the signal.

Thanks for reading.

item.title: MentorAgent: Turn Your .NET Methods into AI Actions Under Your Rules
item.content:encoded:
MentorAgent is an open-source library for .NET 10 that puts an AI agent between your systems and your users, and keeps it under your rules. On one side, the agent uses what you already have: the methods of your .NET application, the tools of MCP servers, other agents over A2A. On the other side, your agent and its actions reach people and programs wherever they are: on the web, on mobile, in AI assistants, in other agents, in scripts and services. In the middle, MentorAgent enforces your rules, splits work among specialists and teams, knows the user’s page, keeps costs in check, shows what happened and runs the model you choose, in the cloud or local.

MentorAgent at a glance

  • Your systems: .NET methods marked with [MentorAction], tools from MCP servers, agents reached over A2A.
  • MentorAgent: six capabilities between the two sides: governance, specialists and teams, pages and skills, cost control, observability, and the model you choose, in the cloud or local.
  • Wherever your users are: web and mobile apps, AI assistants through MCP, other agents through A2A, scripts and services through HTTP and Server-Sent Events.

Why MentorAgent

A chatbot that answers questions is easy to build. An agent that acts inside a business application is not. As soon as it can change data, the questions change too:

  • What can it use: your services, MCP tools, other agents?
  • Who may ask for what, and who confirms changes?
  • How does it split complex work, and how do you see what it did?
  • Which model answers, and what does it cost?
  • Where do users meet it: web, mobile, an AI assistant, another system?

MentorAgent answers each of these in your code, not in the prompt.

Your systems: what the agent can use

.NET methods

The problem. Your services already know how to read an order or issue a refund. Rewriting that logic for an AI framework duplicates it, and the two copies drift apart.

What MentorAgent does. You keep your services. A [MentorAction] attribute marks the methods the agent may use, and one call registers the library, the model and the classes to scan:

using Microsoft.Extensions.AI;
using Novior.MentorAgent.Extensions;
using OpenAI;
 
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
 
// Action classes come from the DI container
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderStore, SqlOrderStore>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();
 
builder.Services.AddMentorAgent(options =>
{
    options.AppName = "ShopFlow back office";
    options.ScanAssemblies = [typeof(Program).Assembly];
    options.ChatClient = new OpenAIClient(builder.Configuration["OpenAI:Key"]!)
        .GetChatClient("gpt-4o-mini")
        .AsIChatClient();
});
 
builder.Services.AddRazorComponents().AddInteractiveServerComponents();

The result. One source of truth for the business logic. The agent calls the same methods your controllers and pages call.

MCP tools and A2A agents

The problem. Useful capabilities often live outside your application: a carrier’s tracking service, a warehouse agent, a tool written in another language.

What MentorAgent does. Two options connect them. McpServers adds tools from MCP servers, optionally limited to an allow list. RemoteAgents adds A2A agents as specialists the coordinator can hand work to. MCP and A2A have official SDKs for Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, Java, C#, Go and Rust, so those tools and agents can be written in any of them.

The result. Your agent works with the rest of your landscape through open standards, not custom integrations. A remote agent runs under its own host’s rules: your roles don’t apply to it, and any user of your agent can reach it.

MentorAgent: six capabilities in the middle

Governance

The problem. “Please ask before refunding” in a prompt is a wish. A model can forget it, misread it, or be talked out of it.

What MentorAgent does. The rules live on the method and are enforced every time a tool is called, outside the model:

using Novior.MentorAgent.Attributes;
 
public class OrderService(IOrderStore store)
{
    [MentorAction(Description = "Returns the status of an order", ReadOnly = true)]
    public Task<string> GetOrderStatus(string orderNumber)
        => store.GetStatusAsync(orderNumber);
 
    [MentorAction(Description = "Refunds an order, fully or in part", RequiredRoles = ["CustomerCare"])]
    public async Task<string> RefundOrder(string orderNumber, decimal amount, string reason)
    {
        await store.RefundAsync(orderNumber, amount, reason);
        return $"Order {orderNumber}: refund of {amount:0.00} registered.";
    }
}
  • Read-only actions run without questions.
  • Every other action asks for confirmation by default, because RequireConfirmationForWrites is on unless you turn it off.
  • The confirmation is concrete: it shows the action with its real arguments, such as the order number and the amount.
  • Roles are checked against the user’s claims, before the confirmation and again after it.
  • The gate travels with the tool, into specialist agents and team members too.
  • Tools you can’t annotate, from MCP servers or skills, can be gated by name with RequiresApproval.

The result. The model proposes; your rules decide. A good way to start is with read-only actions: they are useful from day one and need no confirmation. Write actions follow when the roles are in place.

Read more in governance.

Specialists and teams

The problem. One agent with fifty tools gets confused, and some decisions need more than one look.

What MentorAgent does. Three levels, all declared with attributes:

  • Actions, with [MentorAction].
  • Specialists, with [MentorAgent]: agents with their own instructions and actions, reached through a handoff workflow.
  • Teams, with [MentorTeam] and [TeamMember]: a group chat that approves or rejects a decision. When it approves, the coordinator can route the work to a specialist.

Agents can also be described in YAML with Novior.MentorAgent.Declarative. Everything is built on the handoff and group chat orchestrations of Microsoft Agent Framework.

The result. Focused agents, each with a short list of tools, and decisions that pass through review before anything changes.

Read more in agent levels.

Pages and skills

The problem. An assistant in a box in the corner doesn’t know where the user is, and a long system prompt full of policies costs tokens on every call.

What MentorAgent does.

  • [MentorPage] lets the agent take the user to a page of your app; through IMentorPageContext, the page shares what the user is looking at and offers actions on the interface.
  • [MentorSkill] packages knowledge, such as a return policy, that the model loads only when it needs it (with EnableSkills on).

The result. An agent that feels part of the application, with a smaller context.

Cost control

The problem. Every model call has a price, and an agent makes many.

What MentorAgent does. Each lever is an option, off by default; a dashboard shows the result.

  • Routing between a small model and a strong one, by your rule, by a classifier, by semantic similarity or in cascade (for non-streaming calls).
  • Tool filtering sends only the most relevant actions to the model.
  • Compaction trims long conversations before each call.
  • Rate limits per signed-in user.
  • A Blazor dashboard for usage and cost, with the model prices you configure.

The result. Costs you can see, and levers to keep them down.

Observability

The problem. When an agent calls tools on behalf of users, you need to see what happened, next to the rest of your telemetry.

What MentorAgent does. With EnableObservability, MentorAgent emits OpenTelemetry spans for turns and tool calls, and counters for turns, tool calls, errors and guardrail blocks. Whatever the option, logs of role refusals and MCP calls identify the caller by a fingerprint, not by name. The confirmation events are available for you to record who approved what. The library sends no telemetry of its own to its authors.

The result. The agent shows up in the same traces and dashboards as the rest of your application.

Cloud or local models

The problem. Models change every few months, and some data must not leave the company.

What MentorAgent does. The model is an IChatClient from Microsoft.Extensions.AI: Azure OpenAI and OpenAI, or Ollama and other servers with an OpenAI-compatible API. You can also pass your own Agent Framework AIAgent, such as a Foundry agent; specialists, teams and remote agents are not available in that case. MentorAgent doesn't bundle a provider; you add the package for the one you choose, for example Microsoft.Extensions.AI.OpenAI. With a local model, the conversation and the data your actions read stay inside your network, except what you choose to send to remote MCP servers or agents.

The result. The model becomes a replaceable part, in the cloud or on your own machines, without touching the actions.

Wherever your users are

The problem. Users are in the browser, in a mobile app, in an AI assistant, or are other systems altogether. Building one assistant per channel multiplies the work and the rules.

What MentorAgent does. Your actions and their rules are the same on every channel:

  • Web: Blazor Server and Blazor WebAssembly or Auto get a ready-made <ChatWidget />. React, Angular, Vue or plain JavaScript connect to the SignalR hub with @microsoft/signalr.
  • Mobile: a .NET MAUI app on Android or Windows uses the same widget; native apps use the official SignalR clients for Java on Android and Swift on iOS.
  • AI assistants: as an MCP server, your actions become tools for MCP clients, such as the AI assistants in the IDE or on the desktop.
  • Other agents: as an A2A server, your whole agent becomes a peer that agents written in other languages can call.
  • Scripts and services: where no SignalR client fits, such as a Python script, a shell or a service in another language, Server-Sent Events work with any HTTP client.

On the server, a few calls set up every transport:

using Novior.MentorAgent.Extensions;
using Novior.MentorAgent.Server.Extensions;
 
// In AddMentorAgent: options.McpServerEnabled = true; options.A2AServerEnabled = true;
builder.Services.AddMentorAgentServer();   // hub, SSE, MCP and A2A services
 
var app = builder.Build();
 
app.MapMentorAgentServer(configureTransports: endpoints => endpoints.RequireAuthorization());
app.MapMentorAgentMcp(configure: endpoints => endpoints.RequireAuthorization());
app.MapMentorAgentA2A(configure: endpoints => endpoints.RequireAuthorization());

The rules follow the channel. An MCP client has nobody to click “Confirm”, so MCP publishes only the actions that need no confirmation. Role-protected actions appear only when you identify the caller with McpCallerPrincipal and the caller holds the role. The A2A card leaves out both kinds.

The result. One agent to build and govern, wherever your users are.

Warning: The hub, SSE, MCP and A2A endpoints are open until you protect them. Add your authorization policies as in the example above.

Read more in channels.

Where it runs

MentorAgent is a .NET 10 library that runs inside your application, an ASP.NET Core host or a .NET MAUI app, so it goes wherever that application goes: Windows or Linux, a container, the cloud, or your own servers. The widget loads nothing from third-party servers. The core is .NET; everything around it, from the front ends to the tools and agents it talks to, can be written in other languages.

Where it fits

Existing .NET systems that become AI-ready. Once on .NET 10, a management system, a back office or a customer portal already holds years of business rules. Marking the right service methods is enough to give it an agent, without a rewrite and without a second copy of the logic.

Internal copilots for operators. Customer care, sales, logistics or administration staff ask in plain language and the agent finds the order, the contract or the case, then prepares the next step. Read-only actions answer at once; the actions that change data wait for the operator’s confirmation.

Assistants for end customers. In an online store, a utility’s customer area or a booking portal, customers check the status of an order, a request or a delivery, and start simple operations. Only the actions you choose are visible, and the roles decide who can do what.

Back-office automations with a human in the loop. Refunds, credit notes, address changes, record corrections: the agent prepares the operation with its real arguments, and a person approves it. A team of agents can review the request first, so the operator sees a decision that has already been checked.

Agents that work across companies. A retailer’s agent asks the carrier’s agent where a parcel is; a supplier’s agent checks the stock of a customer. With A2A, each company keeps its own agent, its own rules and its own data, and they talk to each other in natural language. Only actions that need no confirmation are open to the other side, and roles count only for callers you authenticate.

Company tools for employees’ AI clients. Many employees already use AI assistants in the editor or on the desktop. Through MCP, the company’s own actions become tools for those assistants, but only the ones that need no confirmation, and the role-protected ones only for callers you identify.

Software vendors. A team that sells a .NET product can add an agent to it once and offer it to every customer, each installation configured with the customer’s model, in the cloud or on their own servers.

Regulated sectors. Finance, insurance, healthcare and the public sector need to know who did what and why. Roles and confirmations are enforced in code, with EnableObservability every tool call becomes an OpenTelemetry span, every decision on an action, with who confirmed it, can feed your own audit records, and a local model keeps the data at home.

Mobile and field apps. The same agent in a .NET MAUI app on Android or Windows, or in a native app through the Java and Swift SignalR clients.

What becomes possible

When an agent can use the systems a company already has, under the company’s own rules, and reach its users wherever they are, the application gains a new interface, and the business logic a new reach:

  • Every service method is one attribute away from being a capability of the agent, with the same rules for every caller.
  • The same gate on every channel: the widget, a mobile app, a script, an IDE assistant or another company’s agent: roles are checked for every caller, and where nobody can confirm, the actions that need confirmation are not offered.
  • The model becomes a replaceable part: a cloud model today, a local one tomorrow, a small one for easy turns and a strong one for hard ones, without touching the actions.
  • Adoption can grow step by step: read-only actions first, then writes with confirmation, then specialists and teams for the decisions that need them.
  • The systems of a company become reachable by the agents of its partners, through open standards and on its own terms.

What stays in your code

  • Data permissions: MentorAgent checks roles. Which records a user may see or change is decided by your code: in your methods, or in an IMentorActionPolicy that MentorAgent asks before every call.
  • ReadOnly is trusted: if a method marked read-only writes, nothing stops it.
  • Only [MentorAction] has rules: a method exposed with a plain [Description] has no roles and asks no confirmation, unless RequiresApproval names it. A warning lists them the first time MentorAgent reads your actions.
  • Audit: every decision on an action, who confirmed it included, reaches an IMentorActionObserver for you to record. The library doesn't keep an audit store of its own.

What’s next

MentorAgent is the foundation. The project is working on a console to see, try, configure and govern the agents of each application, and on a ready-made installation that runs everything on your own servers, local model included. Each will be announced here when it’s ready.

Follow the updates: the blog’s RSS feed brings every announcement to your feed reader, and on GitHub Watch → Custom → Releases sends you a notification for every new version.

Get started

  • Quickstart: an assistant in a Blazor app, step by step
  • Packages on NuGet: Novior.MentorAgent, plus Novior.MentorAgent.Server for the hub, SSE, MCP and A2A
  • Source on GitHub, under the Apache 2.0 license
  • Documentation: concepts, channels and the full options reference

Written with the help of AI; code and facts checked by the MentorAgent team.

item.title: What a 1.0 Can Honestly Promise
item.content:encoded:
What turned up when a lease library met a real database, a drifting clock, and a call that never returned

This follows a three-part series on checkpointed lease handoff in distributed systems. It stands on its own.

The second article in that series taught a distinction the library implemented incorrectly.

The distinction is between a clean handoff and a crash. worklease coordinates work between processes with leases: locks that expire unless the holder keeps renewing them. A worker that finishes and releases its lease leaves a checkpoint the next owner can trust. A worker that vanishes leaves one the next owner has to validate. Everything downstream depends on telling them apart: whether to continue or reconcile, and whether the work is available now or only after the lease expires.

worklease carried that distinction in a single boolean, and the boolean was wrong in one sequence. Worker A released cleanly. Worker B acquired the lease, started work, and crashed before writing a checkpoint. Worker C acquired it and was told the handoff was clean, because the flag had been inherited from A’s release and only a checkpoint from B would have cleared it. C skipped the validation a crash requires, though B had been working.

That isn’t an exotic failure. It is two ordinary events in a row.

worklease 1.0 has not been run in production. It has been specified, tested on two backends, and audited, but it has not carried real load. That limits what this article can claim, and the limit is stated in full near the end.

Handoff: a flag that described the wrong holder

The fix was not a patch to the boolean. The boolean is gone.

Every holder now declares how it left: finished, abandoned, or retired. The library infers the one exit no holder can declare, which is that the lease expired with no declaration at all. A successor reads how the previous holder exited, not a flag that might describe someone earlier.

The model from the second article held: state is written atomically with the lease renewal, and a fencing counter rejects writes from a holder that has been superseded. What failed was the code around that model. A flag describing the wrong holder was one case. The others were a shutdown path that discarded final state, a renewal loop that trusted a call to return, and a window computed from two clocks.

Shutdown: a path the test double forgave

Three entry points promised the same thing. Runner.Run, Elect, and pool.Run each documented that the lease was released before they returned. The runner, and the pool through it, also wrote a final checkpoint first.

All three did that final work with the caller’s context. On graceful shutdown, that context is already cancelled.

On PostgreSQL, both calls failed before reaching the database. The reproduction takes four steps: a work function waits for cancellation, returns its final state along with the context error, the parent context is cancelled, and the next worker tries to acquire. Run returned context canceled. The next Acquire got ErrLeaseHeld until the full TTL elapsed. When it finally acquired, the final state had never been stored, and the handoff looked like a crash.

Scaled up, that meant every graceful cancellation of pool.Run discarded each slot's final state and held every lease for a full TTL. The orderly path was the failing one.

This was not found by an incident. It was found by reading three docstrings against what the code did, then reproducing the difference on PostgreSQL 16.

The reason nothing had caught it is the part worth keeping. The in-memory backend ignored context cancellation, so a cancelled Release simply worked. Every integration spec ran against it. The test double was kinder than the database, and the spec suite was built on the double.

The fix has two halves. The first is a cleanup context that survives cancellation of the caller’s, bounded by a timeout:

cleanupCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), cleanupTimeout)

The second is that the in-memory backend now honors cancellation the way database/sql does, so the same specs can fail the same way on both backends. The integration suite runs on both, and on PostgreSQL it fails instead of skipping when the database is missing in CI.

What a successor sees after a cancelled shutdown is now specific. It reads the final state, and the previous holder’s exit is recorded as abandoned, not inferred from silence. The work is available immediately, with no wait for the TTL.

That has a price. The cleanup bound defaults to five seconds, and the final checkpoint and the release share it. A shutdown can now run up to five seconds past cancellation. If the database is unreachable and the budget runs out, the exit may go unrecorded, the lease lapses on its own, and the successor sees the exit as expired, the same as a crash. The bound keeps shutdown from hanging, and in return the guarantee is explicitly best-effort.

Renewal: a call that was never allowed to be late

The renewal goroutine kept a lease alive by calling Renew on a timer. It had a retry policy bounded by the lease window, and that bound was checked between attempts.

It was never checked during one.

A Renew that stalled, on a half-open TCP connection or a lock wait in the database, ran with the parent context and no deadline of its own. Two things followed. stopRenewal waited for the goroutine to exit, so it blocked for as long as the call did, and so did Runner.Run and Elect, which call it before releasing. And a single stalled attempt could run past the lease's expiry while the renewal context stayed live, so work kept running under a lease that no longer existed.

It was found by asking what the loop does when a call never returns.

The fix gives every attempt a deadline at the current lease window, and enforces the window on a timer in every wait. When the window closes, the renewal context is cancelled with a specific cause, whether the loop is between ticks, backing off, or stuck inside a call. stopRenewal no longer waits on I/O. An abandoned call is reported to the observer with its context error, and its late result is discarded.

That is not free. An abandoned call is cancelled and ignored, but it is not killed. At most one can outlive stopRenewal per renewal, and on a half-open connection it ends only when TCP keepalive gives up. The goroutine stops waiting, and the connection does not stop being broken.

Time: two clocks, one comparison

Enforcing the window on a timer turned an old assumption into a fatal one.

The first window started at the earlier of two values: the expiry the backend stamped on the lease, and the local start of the acquiring call plus the TTL. One value came from the backend’s clock and the other from the application’s. The window was a comparison between two clocks.

While the window was consulted only after a failed renewal, the comparison rarely mattered: it counted only if the first renewal attempt failed. Once the window was enforced on a timer, it counted every time. A backend clock running behind the application shortened the first window by the skew. A skew above half the TTL cancelled the renewal context before the first renewal. A skew of a full TTL, or a zero or past expiry, cancelled it the moment renewal started, while storage still held a perfectly good lease.

It happened in a development environment. A Podman VM’s clock drifted anywhere from fifteen minutes to three hours behind its host, and every PostgreSQL-backed lease failed with the window-exhausted error. The change that enforced the window and the change that fixed this shipped in the same release, so no released version carried the failure.

The documentation had guarded one direction. From the first release it said the database decides expiry and worker-side clocks play no part in that decision. The renewal code’s own godoc described the first window as the earlier of the two values, then said the local bounds never exceed the true expiry, whatever the skew between the clocks. That was true. It said nothing about a window that came in too short, which is the direction the comparison failed in. The mechanism was written down, and the dependency it created was not. A library that works only when its operators’ clocks agree has not solved clock skew; it has handed the problem to whoever runs it.

The comparison had no safety to give. The backend computes the stored expiry from its own clock when it executes the statement. Provided that clock is steady, that moment is never earlier, in real time, than the moment the client started the call. So the local start plus the TTL can never exceed the true expiry, whatever the offset between the two clocks. The local start is a monotonic reading, so a step in the application’s own wall clock does not move it. All of this holds only if the backend stores at least the TTL it was asked for. Every option that kept the cross-clock comparison left the outage in place, so the comparison went.

The first window is now the local start of the acquiring call plus the TTL, and every later window uses the local clock alone. The assumption didn’t disappear. It moved into the Backend.Acquire contract: the stored expiry is at least the TTL after a reading of the backend's clock taken during the call, rounded up when the backend cannot represent the TTL exactly. Both shipped backends have a spec pinning it. Anyone writing a third has the sentence to check against.

A constant offset in either direction can no longer shorten or extend the window. A database clock that steps forward during a lease, from an NTP correction or a VM resync, or that simply runs fast, still can. The lease can expire in storage while the old holder’s renewal context is live, and a successor can acquire in the gap. Fencing then rejects the old holder’s writes to the lease store.

Promise: what the 1.0 covers, and what it declines

A 1.0 is not a statement that a library is finished. It is a statement about what its authors will not change without telling you, and the useful part is the list of things it declines to promise.

worklease’s list is short, and stricter than “follows semantic versioning.” A change to any exported identifier outside internal/ is breaking, with exceptions that apply only to implementers. Lease and the observer interfaces may gain methods in a minor release. Code that embeds the matching no-op type, or the Lease interface itself, keeps compiling. Code that implements them from scratch does not, and the promise does not cover it. The Backend interface does not grow at all: a new capability arrives as an optional interface found by type assertion, because every backend written against it would otherwise break.

Error message text is not part of the promise. Match the sentinel with errors.Is, and a rewording is a minor-release change the changelog lists. The schema may gain tables, nullable columns, and indexes in a minor release, never lose or rename a column, and the supported Go versions are the two latest releases.

Defaults are easy to leave unsaid. Here each one is classified. Most are tunable: the renewal interval, the retry backoff, the cleanup bound. A tunable default may change in a minor release when the changelog says so, and anyone depending on a value sets it explicitly. A few are frozen, and the freezing is not uniform. In leader, an unset backoff interval means no sleep. In pool, the same field defaults to one second. Both are documented, and neither will change.

The leader one is the more instructive of the two. A one-second default was considered and rejected, because Elect applies the backoff after every return that follows a successful acquire, including a clean finish. A one-shot election would have slept after finishing its work. The cost of keeping zero is that a loop calling Elect against an unreachable database, with the field unset, spins hard against it. The documentation says so and shows the setting that stops it. A default is part of the API, and a frozen default can be wrong for some callers. It has to be stated as a trade-off.

The promise is also uneven in how it is enforced. Since 1.0.1, every pull request compares the exported API against the newest release with gorelease, and the build fails on an incompatible change. That tool counts a method added to an interface as incompatible, so the check accepts exactly the four interfaces the promise lets grow, Lease and the three observers, and on a release branch requires such a method to ship in a minor release. The defaults, the schema rule, and the Go-version rule are policy, held by review and the changelog. A reader deciding how far to trust a 1.0 should know which parts a machine checks.

Evidence: what none of this has been through

Everything above describes what worklease says. This section is about what has been shown.

The conformance suite passes on both backends. The integration suite runs the worker, leader, and pool compositions on both, with PostgreSQL required in CI. A test stalls a renewal on a real half-open connection through a proxy, and it retries once on failure, because the stall reproduces cleanly only under load. The exported API has been audited identifier by identifier.

What has not happened is sustained use. worklease has not been run under real load, with real operators, against a database that has bad days. In CI it runs on one PostgreSQL version through two drivers, lib/pq and pgx v5, and the two cancellation specs expect a different error from each, because pgx times out the connection instead of sending a cancel request. A Redis backend and an etcd backend are possible and unscheduled. The density of fixes in this article could suggest a library that has been through more than it has. The fixes are real, but what they came from was reading code, running tests, and one development VM.

Two limits remain. External side effects are not fenced: a worker that has lost its lease may already have called a payment API or written to a bucket, and ErrFenced protects the lease store only, a boundary the third article drew. And a backend clock that steps forward can still expire a lease early, as described above.

What to ask of a 1.0

Read a library’s 1.0 for what it refuses to promise.

Ask which of its defaults it will change, and which it has frozen even though freezing them costs someone. Ask what it says happens when a call never returns, when the clock is wrong, when shutdown is not orderly. Ask whether its test doubles are as hard on it as its real dependencies are. And ask, of any claim it makes, what it has actually been run against.

worklease v1.0.1 is available at github.com/aetomala/worklease. The compatibility promise is ADR-0020, in docs/adr/.

What a 1.0 Can Honestly Promise was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
